nameStory: The name 'common reed' is wonderfully straightforward - this tall grass has been used to make reeds for musical instruments and thatching for thousands of years. Its scientific name Phragmites comes from the Greek word for 'fence,' referring to how these plants form dense walls of vegetation along waterways.
description: Common reed is a tall, imposing grass that can tower over your head, often reaching 6-15 feet in height. It forms dense colonies of bamboo-like stems topped with large, feathery seed heads that shimmer in the breeze. The long, flat leaves wrap around sturdy, hollow stems, creating an almost tropical look in New England's wetlands. This perennial grass spreads aggressively through underground runners, often dominating entire marshes and pond edges.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms dense, towering colonies that can stretch for acres, with individual stems reaching 6-15 feet tall and swaying together like a golden-brown sea

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Thick, hollow stems (called culms) that feel rigid and bamboo-like when you tap them - they make a satisfying hollow sound and have visible joints or nodes

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Long, flat leaves up to 2 inches wide that wrap around the stem at each joint, with sharp edges that can actually cut your fingers if you're not careful

idTips.label: Seed Heads
idTips.description: Large, fluffy plumes at the top of each stem that start purplish in late summer, then turn tan and feathery, catching and reflecting light beautifully

idTips.label: Roots
idTips.description: Thick, creeping underground stems (rhizomes) that you can sometimes see exposed along shorelines - they feel tough and woody when broken

habitat: Look for common reed in freshwater and brackish wetlands throughout New England - along pond edges, in marshes, roadside ditches, and even in slightly salty coastal areas. It thrives in disturbed, nutrient-rich soils and often dominates areas where the ground stays wet or soggy most of the year. You'll frequently find it growing alongside cattails, though it tends to outcompete most other wetland plants.

seasonality.spring: New green shoots emerge from the mud in late spring, growing rapidly from underground rhizomes. The fresh stems are bright green and surprisingly tender compared to the previous year's tough, tan stalks.
seasonality.summer: Plants reach their full towering height with lush green foliage. By late summer, the distinctive feathery seed heads begin to appear, starting out purplish and compact at the stem tips.
seasonality.fall: The entire colony turns golden-tan and the seed heads become full and fluffy, creating spectacular displays when backlit by autumn sun. Seeds disperse on the wind during this time.
seasonality.winter: Dead stems persist through winter as tall, tan stalks that rattle in the wind. These dried stems are excellent for winter identification, often standing above the snow in distinctive dense patches.

funFact: A single common reed plant can spread over 50 feet in one growing season through its underground runners, and some colonies in Europe are estimated to be over 1,000 years old - making them among the oldest living organisms on Earth!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with cattails, but common reed is much taller with feathery seed heads (not the brown 'hot dog' shape of cattails) and has obvious joints in its stems. Think 'feathers for reeds, hot dogs for cattails' to remember the difference.
contextualKnowledge: Common reed has a complicated reputation - while it's native to New England, aggressive European varieties have invaded and now dominate many wetlands, crowding out native plants and reducing wildlife habitat. The plants you see today are likely these more aggressive introduced forms.
compareHints: Common reed is the only Phragmites species you'll encounter in New England, but it's easily distinguished from other tall wetland grasses by its impressive height, bamboo-like stems with obvious joints, and those characteristic large, feathery seed plumes. Most other wetland grasses are much shorter and have smaller, less showy seed heads.
